## Momentum

**Momentum** (p = mv) measures how much "motion" an object has. It's a vector — direction matters. A 1,400 kg car at 50 km/h carries roughly **19,600 kg·m/s** of momentum, which is why collisions at even moderate speeds are so destructive.

**Units:** kg·m/s (or equivalently, N·s)

---

## Impulse

Impulse is the *change* in momentum, and it equals force × time:

> **J = FΔt = Δp = mΔv**

The crucial insight: **the same change in momentum can be achieved with a huge force for a tiny time, or a moderate force for longer.** This is the physics behind:
- **Crumple zones** — extend collision time → reduce peak force on the driver
- **Airbags** — same principle, padding increases Δt
- **Catching a cricket ball** — "giving" with your hands spreads the impact over more time

---

## Conservation of Momentum

In any closed system (no external forces), total momentum before = total momentum after every collision. This is one of the most fundamental laws in physics. The calculator on the **Conservation** tab lets you verify this with elastic collisions.

Key types: **elastic** (KE conserved, objects bounce), **inelastic** (objects deform, KE lost as heat/sound), **perfectly inelastic** (objects stick together).

| Component | Formula | Key factors |
|---|---|---|
| Thinking distance | v × t_reaction | Speed, fatigue, alcohol, distraction |
| Braking distance | v² / 2a | Speed², road surface, tyre condition |
